title: God with form, God beyond form
hookLine: the goddess asks Bhairava for the real thing, past every description
carry: saguna and nirguna: one God, with and beyond form
tomorrow: where in a single breath is the easiest place to miss?
last: THE BODY, PART OF THE ALTAR.

cards: Ask a friend in love to describe the person and you get a list: funny, kind, great laugh, terrible at directions. All true, and somehow not the person.
In the Vijnana Bhairava, the goddess has heard every list about Bhairava, Shiva in his fierce form. Sound. The phases of a mantra.
The body's energy centers. A goddess's power. She isn't satisfied.

teach.b: Bhairava's answer is startling. Those descriptions, he says, are for beginners, the way a parent coaxes a small child along. They point; they aren't it.
What he is can't be pictured or pinned to a place, beyond direction, time and name.
So the book turns practical and gives doors instead: dharanas, ways of holding the attention. The breath. A fading sound.
A moment of joy. Hindus have two plain words for what's at stake here.

teach.h: SAGUNA: WITH FORM. NIRGUNA: BEYOND IT.
teach.b: Saguna: God with qualities, with a form, a face you can garland.
Nirguna: God beyond every quality and picture. Now let two views inside this path speak. One says: nirguna is the heart of it.
Forms are scaffolding; attention can go straight past them. The other says: careful.

The last days were full of forms, the mantra, the yantra, an image brought to life, and to the people who keep them, a form isn't a child's toy. It's the deity's own presence, a real way in for people who live in bodies.
Many Hindus hold both at once, which is why one family can keep a shrine full of images and still say God is beyond every picture. And notice where this book stands.
Its doors are the breath and the senses, the most ordinary forms there are.
Even this book of the formless walks in through a body.

how: The Vijnana Bhairava is studied in Kashmir Shaiva circles and by meditators, often one practice at a time, with a teacher or in a study group.

o: a list of long temple rites for Bhairava's priests
a tantric book of doors: ways of holding attention
a hymn listing Bhairava's names and his weapons

games.q: the real thing, and the doors. tap the pairs.

s: the Vijnana Bhairava is full of long rites and offering lists
no rites or offering lists: just breath, senses and ordinary moments, used as doors.
in the book, Bhairava calls the descriptions she's heard fit for beginners

games.q: your friend says, 'if God's beyond form, images are childish.' you're asked for the best case of the people who keep the images. what is it?
o: to them the form is the deity's presence, a real way in for embodied people.
images are cheaper than teachers, so they simply reach more people.
images are for children, and adults keep them out of family habit.
games.why: the best case on that side: the mantra, the yantra, the image brought to life aren't toys but presence. and even the Vijnana Bhairava's doors are the breath and the senses.

practice: Look at one simple thing near you for a few breaths: its color, its edges. Then close your eyes and stay with what's left when the picture fades, the plain knowing that was doing the looking.
Move gently between the two for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The Vijnana Bhairava: a small tantric book where the goddess asks for the real thing, and Bhairava answers with doors to try.
